Placement check

Find your level

48 original practice questions, 8 for each of the six levels. Answer what you can, check your answers, and see where to start. Scored in your browser. Nothing is stored or sent.

A self-check, not an assessment. These are practice questions written by Intellica. They are not exam questions, do not predict the result of any external exam and do not count towards any credential. A level counts as familiar at 75% or more.

Level 1: Agentic Cyber Security Foundations

1. A support agent’s reply is changed in transit so a customer is told a refund was approved when it was not. Which security property failed?

Why. Integrity means data and actions are not altered without authorisation. The content changed, and nobody else learned anything secret or lost access.

Review: lesson 1, Security foundations for the agentic era.

2. What is a trust boundary in a threat model?

Why. Threats concentrate where trust changes: user to agent, agent to tool, tool to external service. Drawing those lines is the start of a threat model.

Review: lesson 3, Threat modelling autonomous systems.

3. What does least privilege mean for an agent?

Why. Least privilege limits what a compromised or mistaken agent can do. Logging alone does not limit anything.

Review: lesson 1, Security foundations for the agentic era; lesson 7, Agentic identity and access management.

4. An agent reads a web page while researching. Why should the page text be treated as untrusted?

Why. Content from outside your control can carry instructions. The risk is the model following them, not the format of the page.

Review: lesson 4, Agentic threat landscape and attack patterns; lesson 5, Prompt injection and cognitive exploitation.

5. Which statement correctly separates authentication from authorisation?

Why. An agent must be identified first and then allowed or denied each action. Both apply to agents as well as people.

Review: lesson 7, Agentic identity and access management.

6. What is defence in depth?

Why. Layers should fail independently. Two copies of the same check fail together.

Review: lesson 1, Security foundations for the agentic era.

7. Which describes risk most accurately?

Why. Risk combines threat, weakness, asset, likelihood and impact. A vulnerability alone is not a risk until something valuable and a plausible threat are attached to it.

Review: lesson 1, Security foundations for the agentic era; lesson 3, Threat modelling autonomous systems.

8. An agent’s API key is found in a log file. What should happen first?

Why. Stop further use of the credential, then keep the evidence so you can find out what it was used for. Deleting the log destroys the evidence and the key still works.

Review: lesson 17, Incident response, containment and recovery.

Level 2: Application Cyber Security for Agentic Environments

9. What is indirect prompt injection?

Why. The attacker never talks to the agent directly. They place text where the agent will read it.

Review: lesson 5, Prompt injection and cognitive exploitation.

10. Which control cannot be talked out of its decision by the model?

Why. Enforcement that sits outside the model applies the same rule however the model is persuaded. Instructions and other models are still inside the thing being attacked.

Review: lesson 5, Prompt injection and cognitive exploitation; lesson 14, Runtime enforcement and formal assurance; lesson 22, Out-of-Band Enforcement, and Where It Breaks.

11. What does audience restriction on an access token prevent?

Why. The receiving service checks that the token was meant for it. That blocks passing a token on to another service and a class of confused-deputy attacks.

Review: lesson 26, MCP Authorization: Audience, Discovery and Mix-Up Defence; lesson 7, Agentic identity and access management.

12. How should an agent treat the output of a tool it calls?

Why. Tool output can contain text an attacker controls. Validate it and never let it widen what the agent is allowed to do.

Review: lesson 6, Tool, API and MCP security.

13. A retrieval system serves several customers. Where should access control be enforced?

Why. If a document reaches the model, the model can repeat it. Filter before retrieval returns anything.

Review: lesson 8, Memory, RAG and data security.

14. What is a sound way to run code an agent has generated?

Why. Assume the code is hostile or wrong. Isolation limits what it can reach.

Review: lesson 10, Code execution, sandboxing and isolation.

15. Why verify a model artefact or tool server by digest or signature rather than by name?

Why. Provenance checks tie a decision to exact content. Names and version tags can change underneath you.

Review: lesson 11, AI supply chain and model security; lesson 27, Skills and Tool Trust: The Behavioural Supply Chain.

16. What makes a security test of a control meaningful?

Why. A control must fail closed. A test that only exercises the permitted path cannot show that.

Review: lesson 14, Runtime enforcement and formal assurance; lesson 16, Agentic red teaming and security evaluation.

Level 3: Agentic Security Architect

17. Which design reduces an agent’s agency, not only its privilege?

Why. Agency is how much the agent can decide and do on its own. Approvals and budgets bound it. The other options are good hygiene but do not limit autonomy.

Review: lesson 13, Secure agentic architecture and zero trust; lesson 14, Runtime enforcement and formal assurance.

18. An approval screen shows a description of the action written by the same model that proposed it. What is the main weakness?

Why. The reviewer can only be as accurate as what they are shown. Render the preview from the real call.

Review: lesson 13, Secure agentic architecture and zero trust; lesson 19, Securing agentic AI in critical industries.

19. In a zero-trust design for agents, which statement is right?

Why. Network position is not identity. Each call is verified and evaluated on its own.

Review: lesson 13, Secure agentic architecture and zero trust.

20. What does zero standing privilege mean for an agent?

Why. Standing access is what an attacker inherits. Short-lived, task-scoped grants shrink that.

Review: lesson 28, Agent Identity and Authority: Zero Standing Privilege and Delegation; lesson 7, Agentic identity and access management.

21. Agent A delegates work to agent B by passing its own full credentials. What is wrong with this?

Why. Delegated authority should be attenuated and traceable. Copying credentials spreads a compromise.

Review: lesson 9, Multi-agent security and trust propagation; lesson 28, Agent Identity and Authority: Zero Standing Privilege and Delegation.

22. Which mechanism best limits runaway loops and cost exhaustion in a multi-agent workflow?

Why. Limits must be enforced by something the agents cannot talk around, and they must stop the damage, not only record it.

Review: lesson 9, Multi-agent security and trust propagation; lesson 22, Out-of-Band Enforcement, and Where It Breaks.

23. Which arrangement defeats out-of-band policy enforcement?

Why. If the thing being controlled can change the rules, the control is no longer independent.

Review: lesson 22, Out-of-Band Enforcement, and Where It Breaks.

24. Which is a testable security invariant?

Why. An invariant is a property that must always hold and can be checked. The others cannot be checked or tested directly.

Review: lesson 14, Runtime enforcement and formal assurance; lesson 20, Capstone: design and assure a secure agentic enterprise.

Level 4: Agentic Security Operations Professional

25. To separate what the model said from what was actually executed, which telemetry is essential?

Why. Investigation needs the chain from context to decision to action. The answer text alone does not show what ran.

Review: lesson 15, Monitoring, detection and digital forensics.

26. A detection for suspicious agent behaviour fires constantly on benign long-running tasks. What is the right response?

Why. Detections need evidence of how they behave. Disabling removes the signal; shouting louder adds fatigue.

Review: lesson 15, Monitoring, detection and digital forensics; lesson 25, Runtime Monitors and Honest Detection.

27. An agent you believe is hijacked still holds valid tokens. Which containment step comes first?

Why. Cut off the agent’s ability to act. Restarting or retraining does nothing about live credentials.

Review: lesson 17, Incident response, containment and recovery.

28. Before wiping an agent’s memory store after suspected poisoning, what should you do?

Why. You need the poisoned entries to find the source and the affected sessions. Preserve with integrity, then clean.

Review: lesson 15, Monitoring, detection and digital forensics; lesson 17, Incident response, containment and recovery; lesson 24, Measure Poisoning: Memory, Tool Descriptions and Servers.

29. Why is a monitor model that scores each action not a guarantee?

Why. Detection is probabilistic. Honest detection states what it misses and sits alongside hard controls.

Review: lesson 25, Runtime Monitors and Honest Detection.

30. What is MITRE ATLAS most useful for in detection engineering?

Why. It is a knowledge base of techniques and case studies. Cite a release version when you use it.

Review: lesson 15, Monitoring, detection and digital forensics; lesson 25, Runtime Monitors and Honest Detection.

31. After long-term memory was poisoned and the attack is contained, what must happen before restoring service?

Why. Recovery means removing the cause, closing what it reached and proving it will be caught next time.

Review: lesson 17, Incident response, containment and recovery; lesson 24, Measure Poisoning: Memory, Tool Descriptions and Servers.

32. What is the main privacy risk of logging full prompts and tool results?

Why. Telemetry needs enough detail to investigate without keeping everything forever.

Review: lesson 8, Memory, RAG and data security; lesson 15, Monitoring, detection and digital forensics.

Level 5: Agentic Red Teaming and Assurance Professional

33. Before testing an agent integration that calls a third party’s live API, what do you need?

Why. Permission from the owner of every system touched is the line between testing and attacking.

Review: lesson 16, Agentic red teaming and security evaluation; lesson 23, Contain Your Own Agents and Evaluation Environments.

34. A defence blocks all 200 published jailbreak prompts. What does that show?

Why. Fixed benchmarks measure a past attacker. Real evaluation includes adaptive attacks that respond to the defence.

Review: lesson 21, Break Your Own Defence: Adaptive Evaluation; lesson 16, Agentic red teaming and security evaluation.

35. What makes a finding reproducible?

Why. Someone else must be able to repeat it and see the same thing.

Review: lesson 16, Agentic red teaming and security evaluation.

36. An injected instruction in a retrieved PDF makes the agent try to send internal data to an attacker’s site, but egress policy blocks it. How do you report it?

Why. Report what the attacker achieved and which control held. The injection weakness is still there.

Review: lesson 16, Agentic red teaming and security evaluation; lesson 21, Break Your Own Defence: Adaptive Evaluation.

37. Which is a sound setup for evaluation agents that run attacks?

Why. Contain the test environment as you would hostile code.

Review: lesson 23, Contain Your Own Agents and Evaluation Environments.

38. The model behind an agent is upgraded. What should you re-run?

Why. A change to the model changes behaviour in ways nobody can predict from a version number.

Review: lesson 16, Agentic red teaming and security evaluation; lesson 21, Break Your Own Defence: Adaptive Evaluation.

39. Which check catches a tool description that was changed after you approved it?

Why. Approval applies to specific content. Detect drift from what was reviewed.

Review: lesson 24, Measure Poisoning: Memory, Tool Descriptions and Servers; lesson 27, Skills and Tool Trust: The Behavioural Supply Chain.

40. An attack succeeds on one run in four. How should you report it?

Why. Non-deterministic systems need rates, not single outcomes. A one-in-four success is still a real risk.

Review: lesson 16, Agentic red teaming and security evaluation; lesson 21, Break Your Own Defence: Adaptive Evaluation.

Level 6: Principal Agentic Security and Governance Professional

41. Who should own acceptance of residual risk from an autonomous agent’s actions?

Why. Accountability cannot be delegated to the system or the supplier. Someone with authority signs for what remains.

Review: lesson 18, Governance, regulation and enterprise risk.

42. Which best describes ISO/IEC 42001?

Why. It is organisational. A learner credential does not certify an organisation.

Review: lesson 18, Governance, regulation and enterprise risk.

43. The timetable for high-risk obligations under the EU AI Act changed during 2026. What should a programme do?

Why. Regulatory dates move. Tie each claim to a primary source and a review date.

Review: lesson 18, Governance, regulation and enterprise risk.

44. Which contract term most directly addresses silent changes to a model you depend on?

Why. Behaviour can change without a code change on your side. You need warning and an exit.

Review: lesson 18, Governance, regulation and enterprise risk; lesson 11, AI supply chain and model security.

45. A risk appetite statement for agents should include which of the following?

Why. Appetite becomes operational when it says what is never allowed and what needs which approval.

Review: lesson 18, Governance, regulation and enterprise risk; lesson 19, Securing agentic AI in critical industries.

46. What should a board report on agentic AI emphasise?

Why. Boards act on exposure and decisions, not on technical detail.

Review: lesson 18, Governance, regulation and enterprise risk; lesson 20, Capstone: design and assure a secure agentic enterprise.

47. As of late 2026, how is NIST’s AI Agent Standards Initiative best described?

Why. Teach it as direction of travel and monitor for deliverables. Check the current status before citing it.

Review: lesson 18, Governance, regulation and enterprise risk; lesson 28, Agent Identity and Authority: Zero Standing Privilege and Delegation.

48. Why classify AI use cases by autonomy and tool permissions?

Why. A read-only summariser and an agent that moves money are different risks even if they share a model.

Review: lesson 18, Governance, regulation and enterprise risk; lesson 19, Securing agentic AI in critical industries.
